abstract: |
  This article presents scaling (JS) and aggregated (JSA) James–Stein
  estimation of structural equation models with latent variables, based on 
  their implementation in the R package lavaan. Starting from a worked example, 
  we describe the estimation of factor loadings and latent regression slopes 
  equation by equation, followed by the estimation of variance, covariance, 
  and intercept parameters. We also provide analytical standard errors for 
  JS and JSA using the delta method, accounting for uncertainty across all 
  estimation stages, which were not available before. 
  Throughout, model-implied instrumental-variable (MIIV) estimation serves as
  a point of comparison within a common notation. A simulation study compares
  the standard error accuracy of JS and JSA with that of MIIV and maximum
  likelihood (ML) under correct model specification. The standard errors of
  JS and JSA perform comparably to those of MIIV and ML under the conditions
  examined.

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(lavaan)
library(simhelpers)
library(ggplot2)
library(knitr)
```

Structural equation models (SEMs) with latent variables are usually estimated
by maximum likelihood (ML), which estimates all parameters jointly. Although
ML has desirable asymptotic properties when its assumptions hold
[e.g, @browne_1984], difficulties may arise when it is applied in practice. 
For instance, a misspecification in one equation can
bias estimates in other equations [@kaplan_1988; @bollen_etall_2007;
@bollen_2018; @dhaene_rosseel_2023; see also @jin_etall_2021, for diagonally
weighted least squares], and the iterative optimization can fail to converge
or end in inadmissible solutions, especially in small samples [@bollen_2018;
@dhaene_rosseel_2023]. Equation-by-equation estimators offer an alternative
[e.g., @bollen_1996; @burghgraeve_etall_2021]. With these approaches,
factor loadings and latent regression slopes are estimated one equation at a
time and in closed form, which may limit the propagation of misspecification
across equations [@bollen_gates_fisher_2018; @burghgraeve_etall_2021] and
avoids iterative optimization for this part of the estimation.

This article focuses on James–Stein estimation, an equation-by-equation
estimator proposed for SEMs with latent variables in
@burghgraeve_etall_2021, which replaces each latent predictor by an estimate
of its conditional expectation given observed proxies and then applies
least squares. This conditional expectation is estimated using
James–Stein type shrinkage [@james_stein_1961; @efron_morris_1973;
@efron_morris_1975], and the approach follows the principle of regression
calibration in errors-in-variables regression [@fuller_1987;
@whittemore_1989; @carroll_etall_2006]. James–Stein estimation comes in a
scaling version (JS), which uses the scaling indicators as proxies, and an
aggregated version (JSA), which uses reliability weighted sums of
indicators. Throughout this article, we also use model-implied
instrumental-variable (MIIV) estimation^[Throughout this article, MIIV
refers to model-implied instrumental-variable two-stage least squares
(MIIV-2SLS) estimation [@bollen_1996; @bollen_2018]. Other estimators use
the same model-implied instruments, such as MIIV-GMM
[@bollen_kolenikov_bauldry_2014], which can estimate several equations
jointly, but these are not considered here.] as a point of comparison.
MIIV is one of the more widely known equation-by-equation estimators for
SEMs and also replaces each latent variable by a scaling indicator, but
corrects for the resulting measurement error with instruments implied by
the model rather than with an estimated reliability adjustment
[@bollen_1996; @bollen_bauer_2004; @bollen_2018]. JSA was found to
outperform ML and MIIV in terms of mean squared error under the small
sample conditions examined [@burghgraeve_etall_2021], and both versions
were further evaluated for confirmatory factor models by
@dhaene_rosseel_2024. Placing the two side by side makes clear what JS and
JSA share with MIIV and where they depart from it.

Beyond point estimation, the usefulness of JS and JSA for statistical
inference depends on the accuracy of their standard errors.
@burghgraeve_etall_2021 derived a sampling variance expression for latent
regression estimates that accounts for uncertainty in the estimated
reliability adjustment, providing a basis for analytical standard errors for
those estimates. However, they did not develop a complete analytical
standard error calculation for all model parameters and used bootstrap
standard errors for both JS and JSA in their empirical evaluations. For
MIIV, by contrast, standard errors are well established. Conventional
standard errors for factor loadings and latent regression slopes follow from
two-stage least squares [@bollen_1996]. Standard errors for these same
estimates can also be obtained by the delta method, using derivatives with
respect to the sample moments, for which @fisher_bollen_2020 provided
explicit analytical expressions. These derivatives also propagate
uncertainty in the estimated loadings and slopes into the standard errors of
subsequently estimated variance and covariance parameters. Standard errors
for these latter parameters were derived under unweighted least squares by
@bollen_maydeuolivares_2007 and extended to general weight matrices by
@jin_etall_2021. More recently, @maydeuolivares_etall_2026 compared
subsequent variance and covariance estimation procedures and the accuracy of
their standard errors.

For JS and JSA, this gap has recently been closed in software. The R
package lavaan [@rosseel_2012] now provides analytical standard errors for
both by applying the delta method to the complete estimation procedure. In
addition, its JS and JSA implementations, initially restricted to
confirmatory factor models, have been extended to more general models, and
the package also includes MIIV estimation. Yet neither these analytical
standard errors nor the extended implementations have been systematically
evaluated.

## Present Study and Contributions

This article makes three minor contributions. First, it describes
JS and JSA, as implemented in lavaan, and conceptually compares them with
MIIV estimation within a common notation, starting from a worked
example. Second, it develops and
illustrates a complete delta method calculation of standard errors for JS
and JSA, accounting for uncertainty
across all estimation stages. Third, it evaluates their standard error
accuracy in a simulation study comparing JS and JSA with MIIV and ML.

The remainder of the article introduces the model and notation, presents
the estimators for all parameters together with their analytical standard
errors, and reports the simulation study and its results, followed by a
discussion.

# Model, Notation, and Parameterization

Following the all-y LISREL notation [@joreskog_sorbom_1996, submodel 3B,
Chapter 6; @rosseel_vidal_2025], let $\mathbf y\in\mathbb R^p$ contain the
continuous observed variables and $\boldsymbol\eta\in\mathbb R^q$ the latent
variables. The measurement and latent variable (or structural) models are 
respectively

$$
\mathbf y
=
\boldsymbol\nu+\boldsymbol\Lambda\boldsymbol\eta
+\boldsymbol\epsilon,
\qquad
\boldsymbol\eta
=
\boldsymbol\alpha+\mathbf B\boldsymbol\eta
+\boldsymbol\zeta,
$$
where $\boldsymbol\nu\in\mathbb R^p$ contains the measurement intercepts,
$\boldsymbol\Lambda\in\mathbb R^{p\times q}$ contains the factor loadings,
$\boldsymbol\alpha\in\mathbb R^q$ contains the structural intercepts, and
$\mathbf B\in\mathbb R^{q\times q}$ contains the latent regression slopes,
that is, the regression slopes among the latent variables. The measurement
errors $\boldsymbol\epsilon\in\mathbb R^p$ and structural disturbances
$\boldsymbol\zeta\in\mathbb R^q$ satisfy
$E(\boldsymbol\epsilon)=\mathbf0$ and $E(\boldsymbol\zeta)=\mathbf0$.
Let $\mathbb S_+^m$ and $\mathbb S_{++}^m$ denote the sets of symmetric
positive semidefinite and positive definite $m\times m$ matrices,
respectively. Assume

$$
\operatorname{Var}(\boldsymbol\epsilon)
=
\boldsymbol\Theta\in\mathbb S_+^p,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(\boldsymbol\zeta)
=
\boldsymbol\Psi\in\mathbb S_+^q,
\qquad
\operatorname{Cov}(\boldsymbol\epsilon,\boldsymbol\zeta)
=
\mathbf0_{p\times q}.
$$
Provided that $\mathbf I_q-\mathbf B$ is nonsingular, the latent and
observed mean vectors are

$$
\boldsymbol\mu_\eta
=
(\mathbf I_q-\mathbf B)^{-1}\boldsymbol\alpha
\in\mathbb R^q,
\qquad
\boldsymbol\mu_y
=
\boldsymbol\nu+\boldsymbol\Lambda\boldsymbol\mu_\eta
\in\mathbb R^p,
$$
where $\mathbf I_q$ is the $q\times q$ identity matrix. The implied
observed covariance matrix is

$$
\boldsymbol\Sigma
=
\boldsymbol\Lambda(\mathbf I_q-\mathbf B)^{-1}
\boldsymbol\Psi
(\mathbf I_q-\mathbf B)^{-\top}
\boldsymbol\Lambda^\top
+
\boldsymbol\Theta.
$$ {#eq-implied-covariance}

Let $\boldsymbol\theta\in\mathbb R^d$ collect the free parameters. Assume that $\boldsymbol\Sigma(\boldsymbol\theta)\in\mathbb S_{++}^p$. Denote
the sample mean vector and covariance matrix by
$\overline{\mathbf y}\in\mathbb R^p$ and $\mathbf S\in\mathbb S_+^p$,
respectively, computed from a single group of independent and identically
distributed observations $\mathbf y_i$, $i=1,\ldots,n$, of $\mathbf y$,
which is the setting of all estimation expressions below. Define

$$
\mathbf s
=
\begin{pmatrix}
\overline{\mathbf y}\\
\operatorname{vech}(\mathbf S)
\end{pmatrix}
\in\mathbb R^h,
\qquad
\boldsymbol\sigma(\boldsymbol\theta)
=
\begin{pmatrix}
\boldsymbol\mu_y(\boldsymbol\theta)\\
\operatorname{vech}\{\boldsymbol\Sigma(\boldsymbol\theta)\}
\end{pmatrix}
\in\mathbb R^h,
\qquad
h=p+\frac{p(p+1)}2,
$$
where $\operatorname{vech}$ stacks the lower triangular entries, including
the diagonal. A common choice for estimating $\boldsymbol\theta$ jointly is 
ML, which requires further distributional assumptions
[@browne_1974; @shapiro_2007; see @bollen_2026, Chapter 4, pp. 201--203,
Chapter 5, pp. 352--353, for an overview]. JS, JSA, and MIIV proceed
differently. They first estimate the factor loadings and latent regression
slopes equation by equation, and then the remaining parameters conditional
on these estimates.

# Estimation of Factor Loadings and Latent Regression Slopes

We use a scaling indicator parameterization
[@bollen_1996; @bollen_2018; @burghgraeve_etall_2021], fixing one loading
per latent variable to one and the corresponding intercept to zero
[@bollen_1989]. Each scaling indicator is assumed to load only on its
corresponding latent variable. The loadings and slopes are obtained from
the sample covariances, with intercepts estimated subsequently. The
following example illustrates how JS and MIIV address measurement error in
a scaling indicator used as predictor.

\begin{lsamexample}[A factor loading and a latent regression slope].\label{ex:loading}
Consider four indicators of $\eta_1$, with $y_1$ as its scaling indicator,
so that $y_1=\eta_1+\epsilon_1$ and $y_r=\nu_r+\lambda_r\eta_1+\epsilon_r$
for $r=2,3,4$. Assume $E(\epsilon_r)=0$,
$\operatorname{Cov}(\eta_1,\epsilon_r)=0$, and
$\operatorname{Cov}(\epsilon_r,\epsilon_s)=0$ for $r\ne s$. The objective is to estimate $\lambda_2$. Writing
$\psi=\operatorname{Var}(\eta_1)$ and
$\omega_1=\operatorname{Var}(\epsilon_1)$, the population slope from
regressing $y_2$ directly on $y_1$ is
$$
\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(y_1,y_2)}
     {\operatorname{Var}(y_1)}
=
\lambda_2\frac{\psi}{\psi+\omega_1}.
$$
Thus, measurement error in $y_1$ attenuates the slope. JS estimates the
latent predictor from its scaling indicator. Under joint normality, it can be 
shown that 
$$
E(\eta_1\mid y_1)
=
\mu_1+R(y_1-\mu_1),
\qquad
R=\frac{\psi}{\psi+\omega_1},
$$
where $\mu_1=E(\eta_1)=E(y_1)$ (Burghgraeve et al., 2021). The other indicators 
provide information about $\omega_1$, because
$\operatorname{Cov}(y_1,y_3)=\lambda_3\psi$,
$\operatorname{Cov}(y_1,y_4)=\lambda_4\psi$, and
$\operatorname{Cov}(y_3,y_4)=\lambda_3\lambda_4\psi$. Consequently,
$$
\psi
=
\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(y_1,y_3)\operatorname{Cov}(y_1,y_4)}
     {\operatorname{Cov}(y_3,y_4)},
\qquad
\widehat\omega_1
=
s_{11}-\frac{s_{13}s_{14}}{s_{34}},
$$
where $s_{rs}$ denotes a sample covariance. This is the preliminary error
variance estimate from one pair of other indicators. With the small sample
correction used in JS, the estimated reliability adjustment and fitted
latent predictor are
$$
\widehat R
=
\frac{s_{11}-c_n\widehat\omega_1}{s_{11}},
\qquad
c_n=\frac{n-3}{n-1},
\qquad
\widetilde\eta_1
=
\overline y_1+\widehat R(y_1-\overline y_1).
$$
Regressing $y_2$ on $\widetilde\eta_1$, with an intercept, gives
$$
\widehat\lambda_{2,\mathrm{JS}}
=
\frac{\widehat R\,s_{12}}{\widehat R^2s_{11}}
=
\frac{s_{12}}{s_{11}-c_n\widehat\omega_1}.
$$

MIIV instead substitutes $\eta_1=y_1-\epsilon_1$ into the equation for
$y_2$ (Bollen, 1996), giving $y_2=\nu_2+\lambda_2y_1+u$ with
$u=\epsilon_2-\lambda_2\epsilon_1$. The explanatory variable $y_1$
correlates with the composite error, $\operatorname{Cov}(y_1,u)=-\lambda_2\omega_1$,
whereas $y_3$ satisfies $\operatorname{Cov}(y_3,u)=0$. It can therefore
serve as an instrument when $\operatorname{Cov}(y_3,y_1)\ne0$, giving
$$
\operatorname{Cov}(y_3,y_2)
=
\lambda_2\operatorname{Cov}(y_3,y_1),
\qquad
\widehat\lambda_{2,\mathrm{MIIV}}
=
\frac{s_{32}}{s_{31}}.
$$
With several instruments, such as $y_3$ and $y_4$, two-stage least squares
first regresses $y_1$ on the instruments and then regresses $y_2$ on the
fitted values, including intercepts in both regressions.

The same steps apply to a latent regression slope. In the model used in
the simulation study below, $\eta_2=\alpha_2+B_{21}\eta_1+\zeta_2$ and
$y_5=\eta_2+\epsilon_5$. Substitution gives
$y_5=\alpha_2+B_{21}\eta_1+\zeta_2+\epsilon_5$, which has the form of the equation for $y_2$, with $\zeta_2+\epsilon_5$
in place of $\epsilon_2$. Because $\zeta_2$ and $\epsilon_5$ are
uncorrelated with $\eta_1$ and with $\epsilon_1,\ldots,\epsilon_4$, the
same calculations give
$$
\widehat B_{21,\mathrm{JS}}
=
\frac{s_{15}}{s_{11}-c_n\widehat\omega_1},
\qquad
\widehat B_{21,\mathrm{MIIV}}
=
\frac{s_{35}}{s_{31}}.
$$

Moreover, for either estimator,
$\widehat\nu_2=\overline y_2-\widehat\lambda_2\overline y_1$ and
$\widehat\alpha_2=\overline y_5-\widehat B_{21}\overline y_1$.
Despite not shown in this example, we note JSA follows the JS calculation 
using a normalized aggregate of eligible indicators in place of $y_1$, 
as described below. 
\end{lsamexample}

## James–Stein Estimation

We now present the general expressions behind this example. They concern
free loadings and slopes without equality constraints. All inverses and
ratios are assumed well defined.

### Scaling James–Stein Estimation

Let $\mathbf f\in\mathbb R^k$ collect the latent predictors of the
equation to be estimated, and let $\mathbf x\in\mathbb R^k$ collect their
scaling indicators in matching order. These are selected elements of
$\boldsymbol\eta$ and $\mathbf y$, respectively. Because the scaling
indicators have zero intercepts, unit loadings, and no cross loadings,
their measurement equations reduce to

$$
\mathbf x=\mathbf f+\mathbf e,
$$
where $\mathbf e\in\mathbb R^k$ contains the corresponding measurement
errors. In the example, $f=\eta_1$, $x=y_1$, and $e=\epsilon_1$. Define

$$
\boldsymbol\mu=E(\mathbf f)=E(\mathbf x)\in\mathbb R^k,
\qquad
\boldsymbol\Sigma_x=\operatorname{Var}(\mathbf x)\in\mathbb S_{++}^k,
\qquad
\boldsymbol\Omega=\operatorname{Var}(\mathbf e)\in\mathbb S_+^k.
$$
Assume diagonal $\boldsymbol\Omega$ and
$\operatorname{Cov}(\mathbf f,\mathbf e)=\mathbf0$. Under joint normality,

$$
E(\mathbf f\mid\mathbf x)
=
\boldsymbol\mu+\mathbf R(\mathbf x-\boldsymbol\mu),
\qquad
\mathbf R
=
(\boldsymbol\Sigma_x-\boldsymbol\Omega)\boldsymbol\Sigma_x^{-1}
\in\mathbb R^{k\times k}.
$$ {#eq-conditional-expectation}
Otherwise, @eq-conditional-expectation gives the best linear predictor [@burghgraeve_etall_2021].
The preliminary error variance calculation illustrated in the example
generalizes to

$$
\widehat\omega_j
=
s_{jj}-\frac{s_{js}s_{jt}}{s_{st}},
$$
for three distinct indicators $y_j,y_s,y_t$ loading only on the same
latent variable and having mutually uncorrelated measurement errors.
Estimates are averaged over all such pairs, with bounds applied to the
corresponding estimated communalities. The resulting
scaling indicator error variances form diagonal
$\widehat{\boldsymbol\Omega}\in\mathbb R^{k\times k}$ and need not equal
the final model estimates.

Using the sample covariance matrix $\mathbf S_x\in\mathbb S_{++}^k$ of the
proxies $\mathbf x$, the estimated reliability adjustment and fitted
predictors are

$$
\widehat{\mathbf R}
=
(\mathbf S_x-c_n\widehat{\boldsymbol\Omega})\mathbf S_x^{-1},
\qquad
c_n=\frac{n-3}{n-1},
$$
and
$\widetilde{\mathbf f}=\overline{\mathbf x}+\widehat{\mathbf R}(\mathbf x-\overline{\mathbf x})$.

These fitted latent predictors are then used to estimate one measurement
model or latent variable model equation. Let $\mathbf a\in\mathbb R^k$
contain the corresponding loadings or slopes. The response is the
dependent indicator for a measurement model equation or the dependent
latent variable's scaling indicator for a latent variable model equation.
Let $\delta$ denote its error: $\epsilon_2$ for response $y_2$ and
$\zeta_2+\epsilon_5$ for response $y_5$ in the example. Assume $\operatorname{Cov}(\mathbf f,\delta)=\mathbf0$ and
$\operatorname{Cov}(\mathbf e,\delta)=\mathbf0$. Let $\mathbf X\in\mathbb R^{n\times k}$ contain the centered proxy
observations, with rows $(\mathbf x_i-\overline{\mathbf x})^\top$, and let
$\mathbf d\in\mathbb R^n$ contain the centered response observations. The centered fitted
predictor matrix is $\widetilde{\mathbf X}=\mathbf X\widehat{\mathbf R}^{\top}$,
giving

$$
\widehat{\mathbf a}_{\mathrm{JS}}
=
(\widetilde{\mathbf X}^{\top}\widetilde{\mathbf X})^{-1}
\widetilde{\mathbf X}^{\top}\mathbf d
=
(\mathbf S_x-c_n\widehat{\boldsymbol\Omega})^{-1}\mathbf s_{xd},
$$ {#eq-js-estimator}
where $\mathbf s_{xd}\in\mathbb R^k$ contains the sample covariances
between proxies and response.

### Aggregated James–Stein Estimation

JSA replaces each scaling indicator by a normalized, reliability weighted
aggregate [@burghgraeve_etall_2021]. Eligible indicators load only on the
corresponding latent predictor. Their measurement errors are mutually
uncorrelated across all selected indicators and uncorrelated with
$\delta$, excluding the dependent indicator from its own predictor
aggregate.

For each latent predictor $f$ in $\mathbf f$, let $\mathbf y_f\in\mathbb R^r$
contain its eligible indicators, with intercepts
$\boldsymbol\nu_f\in\mathbb R^r$, loadings
$\boldsymbol\lambda_f\in\mathbb R^r$, and diagonal measurement error
covariance matrix $\mathbf Q_f\in\mathbb S_+^r$. For weights
$\mathbf w\in\mathbb R^r$,

$$
g
=
\frac{\mathbf w^\top(\mathbf y_f-\boldsymbol\nu_f)}
     {\mathbf w^\top\boldsymbol\lambda_f}
=
f+e_g,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(e_g)
=
\frac{\mathbf w^\top\mathbf Q_f\mathbf w}
     {(\mathbf w^\top\boldsymbol\lambda_f)^2},
$$
where $e_g$ is the aggregate's measurement error. Using preliminary error
variance estimates $\widehat{\mathbf Q}_f$ and
sample covariance matrix $\mathbf S_f\in\mathbb S_{++}^r$, the weights
maximize estimated reliability:

$$
\widehat{\mathbf w}
\in
\underset{\mathbf w\ne\mathbf0}{\arg\max}
\left(
1-
\frac{\mathbf w^\top\widehat{\mathbf Q}_f\mathbf w}
     {\mathbf w^\top\mathbf S_f\mathbf w}
\right).
$$
With preliminary scaling JS loadings $\widehat{\boldsymbol\lambda}_f$, the
centered aggregate and its estimated error variance are

$$
\widehat g
=
\frac{\widehat{\mathbf w}^{\top}
      (\mathbf y_f-\overline{\mathbf y}_f)}
     {\widehat{\mathbf w}^{\top}\widehat{\boldsymbol\lambda}_f},
\qquad
\widehat\omega_g
=
\frac{\widehat{\mathbf w}^{\top}\widehat{\mathbf Q}_f\widehat{\mathbf w}}
     {(\widehat{\mathbf w}^{\top}\widehat{\boldsymbol\lambda}_f)^2},
$$
assuming a nonzero normalization denominator.

The centered aggregates replace the columns of $\mathbf X$, and their error
variance estimates form the diagonal of $\widehat{\boldsymbol\Omega}$, in
matching order. Recomputing $\mathbf S_x$ and $\mathbf s_{xd}$ from these
aggregates and applying @eq-js-estimator gives
$\widehat{\mathbf a}_{\mathrm{JSA}}$, with the same response. Thus, JS and JSA
share @eq-js-estimator and differ in the construction of the proxies
and their measurement error variances [@burghgraeve_etall_2021].

## Model-Implied Instrumental-Variable Estimation

For MIIV, $\mathbf x$ and $\mathbf X$ again denote the scaling indicators
and their centered observations. Substituting $\mathbf f=\mathbf x-\mathbf e$
produces the composite error $u=\delta-\mathbf a^\top\mathbf e$. After
centering and stacking observations [@bollen_1996],
$\mathbf d=\mathbf X\mathbf a+\mathbf u$, where $\mathbf u\in\mathbb R^n$
contains the centered composite errors.

The model identifies instruments $\mathbf z\in\mathbb R^\ell$ satisfying
the validity and relevance conditions
$\operatorname{Cov}(\mathbf z,u)=\mathbf0$,
$\operatorname{rank}\{\operatorname{Cov}(\mathbf z,\mathbf x)\}=k$, and
$\ell\geq k$. Let $\mathbf Z\in\mathbb R^{n\times\ell}$ contain their centered
observations. Regressing the explanatory variables on the instruments
gives

$$
\widehat{\mathbf X}
=
\mathbf P\mathbf X,
\qquad
\mathbf P
=
\mathbf Z(\mathbf Z^\top\mathbf Z)^{-1}\mathbf Z^\top
\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}.
$$
Regressing the response on these fitted values then gives

$$
\widehat{\mathbf a}_{\mathrm{MIIV}}
=
(\widehat{\mathbf X}^{\top}\widehat{\mathbf X})^{-1}
\widehat{\mathbf X}^{\top}\mathbf d
=
(\mathbf X^\top\mathbf P\mathbf X)^{-1}\mathbf X^\top\mathbf P\mathbf d.
$$

Both approaches regress the response on fitted predictors. JS and JSA
obtain them through an estimated reliability adjustment, whereas MIIV
projects the scaling indicators onto model-implied instruments.

# Estimation of Variance, Covariance, and Intercept Parameters

After estimating the factor loadings and latent regression slopes, the
remaining variance and covariance parameters can be estimated using several
least squares procedures [see @maydeuolivares_etall_2026, for a comparison
of such procedures with MIIV]. For JS, JSA, and
MIIV, we use reweighted least squares, the default in the implementations
considered, holding the estimated loadings and slopes fixed.

Substituting these estimates into @eq-implied-covariance gives

$$
\boldsymbol\Sigma(\mathbf v)
=
\widehat{\mathbf H}\boldsymbol\Psi(\mathbf v)
\widehat{\mathbf H}^{\top}
+
\boldsymbol\Theta(\mathbf v),
\qquad
\widehat{\mathbf H}
=
\widehat{\boldsymbol\Lambda}
(\mathbf I_q-\widehat{\mathbf B})^{-1}
\in\mathbb R^{p\times q},
$$
assuming that $\mathbf I_q-\widehat{\mathbf B}$ is nonsingular. Here,
$\mathbf v\in\mathbb R^{d_v}$ collects the free variance and covariance
parameters in $\boldsymbol\Theta$ and $\boldsymbol\Psi$. With
$\widehat{\mathbf H}$ held fixed, the implied covariance moments are linear
in $\mathbf v$ [@browne_1974; @ernst_etall_2023], that is,
$\operatorname{vech}\{\boldsymbol\Sigma(\mathbf v)\}=\widehat{\mathbf c}+\widehat{\mathbf G}\mathbf v$.
Here, $t=p(p+1)/2$, $\widehat{\mathbf c}\in\mathbb R^t$ contains the fixed
component, and $\widehat{\mathbf G}\in\mathbb R^{t\times d_v}$ maps the
free parameters to the implied moments, incorporating any linear equality
restrictions.

For a weight matrix $\widehat{\mathbf W}\in\mathbb S_{++}^t$,

$$
\widehat{\mathbf v}
=
(\widehat{\mathbf G}^{\top}\widehat{\mathbf W}\widehat{\mathbf G})^{-1}
\widehat{\mathbf G}^{\top}\widehat{\mathbf W}
\left\{\operatorname{vech}(\mathbf S)-\widehat{\mathbf c}\right\},
$$ {#eq-wls}
assuming full column rank of $\widehat{\mathbf G}$. 
Reweighted least squares updates the normal theory weights using the
current implied covariance matrix [@browne_1974; @lee_jennrich_1979]:

$$
\widehat{\mathbf W}^{(\tau)}
=
\frac12\mathbf D_p^\top
\left[
\{\widehat{\boldsymbol\Sigma}^{(\tau)}\}^{-1}
\otimes
\{\widehat{\boldsymbol\Sigma}^{(\tau)}\}^{-1}
\right]\mathbf D_p,
\qquad
\widehat{\boldsymbol\Sigma}^{(\tau)}
=
\boldsymbol\Sigma(\widehat{\mathbf v}^{(\tau)}).
$$
Here, $\otimes$ denotes the Kronecker product, and
$\mathbf D_p\in\mathbb R^{p^2\times t}$ is the duplication matrix
satisfying
$\operatorname{vec}(\mathbf S)=\mathbf D_p\operatorname{vech}(\mathbf S)$.
Substituting $\widehat{\mathbf W}^{(\tau)}$ into @eq-wls gives
$\widehat{\mathbf v}^{(\tau+1)}$. This procedure continues
until convergence, assuming positive definite implied covariance matrices
throughout. The resulting $\widehat{\boldsymbol\Theta}$ and
$\widehat{\boldsymbol\Psi}$ are not constrained to be positive
semidefinite.

Finally, intercepts are estimated from the sample means. When all
nonscaling indicator intercepts and structural intercepts are free, the
mean structure is saturated. Let $\overline{\mathbf m}\in\mathbb R^q$
contain the sample scaling indicator means, ordered by latent variable.
Then

$$
\widehat{\boldsymbol\mu}_\eta
=
\overline{\mathbf m},
\qquad
\widehat{\boldsymbol\nu}
=
\overline{\mathbf y}
-
\widehat{\boldsymbol\Lambda}\overline{\mathbf m}
\in\mathbb R^p,
\qquad
\widehat{\boldsymbol\alpha}
=
(\mathbf I_q-\widehat{\mathbf B})\overline{\mathbf m}
\in\mathbb R^q.
$$ {#eq-intercepts}
The expressions in @eq-intercepts preserve the fixed zero scaling indicator intercepts and
reproduce the sample means. Additional mean structure restrictions are
accommodated by generalized least squares, fitting
$\boldsymbol\mu_y=\boldsymbol\nu+\widehat{\mathbf H}\boldsymbol\alpha$ to
$\overline{\mathbf y}$ under those restrictions, with weight matrix
$\widehat{\boldsymbol\Sigma}^{-1}$ where
$\widehat{\boldsymbol\Sigma}=\boldsymbol\Sigma(\widehat{\mathbf v})$.

Together, these stages estimate the free entries of $\boldsymbol\Lambda$,
$\mathbf B$, $\boldsymbol\Theta$, $\boldsymbol\Psi$, $\boldsymbol\nu$, and
$\boldsymbol\alpha$. Although loadings and slopes are held fixed during
covariance estimation, their sampling uncertainty is included in the
standard error calculations.

# Analytical Standard Errors

## James–Stein Estimation

@burghgraeve_etall_2021 derived a variance expression for latent regression
slopes accounting for the estimated reliability adjustment and used
bootstrap standard errors in their evaluations. Here, analytical standard
errors follow from differentiating the complete estimation procedure with
respect to the sample moments. For $T\in\{\mathrm{JS},\mathrm{JSA}\}$,
write $\widehat{\boldsymbol\theta}_T=g_{n,T}(\mathbf s)$, where $g_{n,T}$ maps the $h$ sample moments to the $d$ parameter estimates
through the estimation stages described above.

Suppose

$$
\sqrt n\{\mathbf s-\boldsymbol\sigma(\boldsymbol\theta)\}
\xrightarrow{d}
N_h(\mathbf0,\boldsymbol\Gamma),
\qquad
\boldsymbol\Gamma\in\mathbb S_+^h,
$$
where $\boldsymbol\Gamma$ is the joint asymptotic covariance matrix of the
sample means and covariances. Under the required moment and
differentiability conditions,

$$
\widehat{\mathbf V}_T
=
\frac1n
\widehat{\mathbf J}_T
\widehat{\boldsymbol\Gamma}
\widehat{\mathbf J}_T^\top
\in\mathbb S_+^d,
\qquad
\widehat{\mathbf J}_T
=
\left.
\frac{\partial g_{n,T}(\mathbf s)}
     {\partial\mathbf s^\top}
\right|_{\mathbf s=\mathbf s_{\mathrm{obs}}}
\in\mathbb R^{d\times h}.
$$

The Jacobian propagates uncertainty through all stages, including the
preliminary error variances and intercept estimates. It is evaluated
analytically by default, using implicit differentiation for the converged
reweighted least squares equations. For JSA, it also includes derivatives
of the aggregation weights and normalization loadings.

The matrix $\boldsymbol\Gamma$ can be estimated using normal theory or
empirical moments through order four [@browne_1984]. Normal theory
estimates may use the sample or fitted covariance matrix. For parameter
$j=1,\ldots,d$,
$\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(\widehat\theta_{T,j})=\sqrt{[\widehat{\mathbf V}_T]_{jj}}\in[0,\infty)$.

## Model-Implied Instrumental-Variable Estimation

For the MIIV loadings and slopes in one equation, the default
homoskedastic covariance estimator is
$\widehat{\mathbf V}_{\mathbf a,\mathrm{MIIV}}=\widehat\sigma_u^{\,2}(\mathbf X^\top\mathbf P\mathbf X)^{-1}\in\mathbb S_+^k$,
where

$$
\widehat\sigma_u^{\,2}
=
\frac{\widehat{\mathbf u}^{\top}\widehat{\mathbf u}}
     {n-k-1},
\qquad
\widehat{\mathbf u}
=
\mathbf d-\mathbf X\widehat{\mathbf a}_{\mathrm{MIIV}}.
$$
Centering absorbs the intercept, and $n>k+1$ is assumed. Here,
$\sigma_u^2$ is the composite error variance, rather than an individual
measurement error or structural disturbance variance. Alternatively, moment 
based standard errors for the MIIV loadings and
slopes follow from the delta method. Let $d_a$ denote their total number
and let $\widehat{\mathbf K}\in\mathbb R^{d_a\times t}$ be the Jacobian of
their estimates with respect to $\operatorname{vech}(\mathbf S)$
[@fisher_bollen_2020]. Their estimated covariance matrix is

$$
\frac1n
\widehat{\mathbf K}
\widehat{\boldsymbol\Gamma}_S
\widehat{\mathbf K}^{\top},
$$
where $\widehat{\boldsymbol\Gamma}_S\in\mathbb S_+^t$ is the
covariance-moment block of $\widehat{\boldsymbol\Gamma}$ for the MIIV fit.

The Jacobian $\widehat{\mathbf K}$ also enters the standard error
calculation for the subsequently estimated variance and covariance
parameters, accounting for uncertainty in the previously estimated
loadings and slopes [@bollen_maydeuolivares_2007; @jin_etall_2021].
Define

$$
\widehat{\mathbf M}
=
(\widehat{\mathbf G}^{\top}\widehat{\mathbf W}\widehat{\mathbf G})^{-1}
\widehat{\mathbf G}^{\top}\widehat{\mathbf W}
\in\mathbb R^{d_v\times t},
$$
evaluated at the converged weights and treated as fixed in the
linearization. Let $\widehat{\boldsymbol\Delta}_1\in\mathbb R^{t\times d_a}$
be the Jacobian of the implied covariance moments with respect to the
loadings and slopes, evaluated at the estimates. Under correct
specification [@bollen_maydeuolivares_2007; @jin_etall_2021],

$$
\widehat{\mathbf V}_{\mathbf v,\mathrm{MIIV}}
=
\frac1n
\widehat{\mathbf M}
(\mathbf I_t-\widehat{\boldsymbol\Delta}_1\widehat{\mathbf K})
\widehat{\boldsymbol\Gamma}_S
(\mathbf I_t-\widehat{\boldsymbol\Delta}_1\widehat{\mathbf K})^\top
\widehat{\mathbf M}^\top
\in\mathbb S_+^{d_v}.
$$
Hence, note the factor
$\mathbf I_t-\widehat{\boldsymbol\Delta}_1\widehat{\mathbf K}$ propagates
uncertainty in the estimated loadings and slopes through the residual
covariance moments. For intercepts, moment based standard errors follow by 
differentiating the
mean structure expressions. These calculations apply the delta method
separately to each parameter block. The second stage linearization holds
the converged weights fixed, whereas the JS and JSA Jacobians differentiate
the complete estimation procedure. A related delta method calculation for
instrumental variable regression is presented by
@maydeuolivares_etall_2019.

# Simulation Design and Performance Evaluation

In this section we describe the design of the simulation study and the
measures used to evaluate the standard errors.

### Population Model and Estimands

We study the model in @fig-model, with three latent variables and four
indicators each. The latent variable model is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\eta_{2}&=\alpha_2+B_{21}\eta_{1}+\zeta_{2},\\
\eta_{3}&=\alpha_3+B_{31}\eta_{1}+B_{32}\eta_{2}+\zeta_{3}.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-pop-structural}

The design is partly based on previous studies. The measurement models
follow the simulations of @burghgraeve_etall_2021, with four indicators per
latent variable and a common reliability of .6 or .8 for all indicators.
The structural model follows their empirical illustration, which has the
same two structural equations. Moreover, 
@jin_etall_2021 used a recursive latent variable model with several equations 
and standardized slopes between 0.1 and 0.6, 
which the present model follows partly with $B_{21}=0.6$, $B_{31}=0.3$, and
$B_{32}=0.5$. The disturbance variances were chosen so that all latent
variables have unit variance. With $\operatorname{Var}(\eta_1)=1$, setting
$\operatorname{Var}(\zeta_2)=0.64$ and $\operatorname{Var}(\zeta_3)=0.48$
gives $\operatorname{Var}(\eta_2)=\operatorname{Var}(\eta_3)=1$. The slopes
therefore equal their standardized values. The implied correlations are .60 
between $\eta_1$ and $\eta_2$,
.60 between $\eta_1$ and $\eta_3$, and .68 between $\eta_2$ and $\eta_3$. 
The scaling indicators have loadings fixed to one and the
remaining loadings range from 0.8 to 1.2. The mean structure has
$E(\eta_1)=1$, $\alpha_2=\alpha_3=0.5$, and $\nu_j=0.2$ for the
nonscaling indicators, where $j$ indexes the indicators in @fig-model. 
The main estimands are all free factor
loadings, latent regression slopes, measurement error variances, and latent 
variances and disturbance variances.


### Simulation Conditions and Estimation Approaches

We employed a fully factorial design with two factors: sample size
($n\in\{100, 200, 300, 400, 500, 600\}$) and indicator reliability
($\rho\in\{.6, .8\}$). This yielded $6\times2=12$ conditions, each
replicated 1,500 times. The sample sizes cover the small to moderate range
in which the equation-by-equation estimators are expected to differ most
from ML [e.g., @burghgraeve_etall_2021; @jin_etall_2021; @dhaene_rosseel_2024]. 
The reliability levels match the low and high
conditions of @burghgraeve_etall_2021, as mentioned before, and determine the 
size of the reliability adjustment in JS and JSA. 

### Data Generation

Data were generated from the population model with all stochastic
components normal and mutually independent. The exogenous latent variable
was generated as $\eta_1\sim\mathcal{N}(1,1)$ and the structural
disturbances as $\zeta_2\sim\mathcal{N}(0,0.64)$ and
$\zeta_3\sim\mathcal{N}(0,0.48)$, from which $\eta_2$ and $\eta_3$ follow
by @eq-pop-structural. The measurement error of each indicator was
generated as $\epsilon_j\sim\mathcal{N}\{0,\lambda_j^2(1-\rho)/\rho\}$,
where $\lambda_j$ is the loading of indicator $j$. This entails that every
indicator has reliability $\rho\in\{.6,.8\}$ in its condition. The indicators 
were then obtained from the measurement equations 
$y_j=\nu_j+\lambda_j\eta_l+\epsilon_j$,
where $\eta_l$ is the latent variable measured by indicator $j$ in
@fig-model, with $\nu_j=0$ and $\lambda_j=1$ for the scaling indicators. 
The observed variables are therefore multivariate
normal with the mean vector and covariance matrix implied by the
population values. 

### Convergence, Outliers, and Inadmissible Solutions

Replications were screened in two steps, and a replication that failed
either step for any estimator was removed for all four. A solution was
nonconverged when any estimate, standard error, or confidence interval
bound of an estimand was missing or non-finite. Among the converged
replications, outliers were point estimates more than three interquartile
ranges below the first or above the third quartile, per condition,
estimator, and estimand. Inadmissible
solutions, with a nonpositive estimate of a measurement error, latent, or
disturbance variance, were retained and counted.

### Performance Measures

Performance was assessed with the measures implemented in the simhelpers
package [@joshi_pustejovsky_2025], computed for every estimand. These
measures, with their empirical and Monte Carlo standard error (MCSE)
calculations, are listed in @tbl-performance. Jackknife MCSEs are used
for the empirical standard deviation (SD) of the estimates and for the
ratio of the mean squared standard error (SE$^2$) to the empirical variance
(VAR). The MCSE of coverage is available in closed form. The SE/SD ratio
and the SE$^2$/VAR ratio compare the same quantities on the standard
deviation and on the variance scale. Only the latter, for which an MCSE is
available, is shown in the figures.
Coverage between .925 and .975 and SE$^2$/VAR ratios between 0.90 and 1.10
were considered acceptable.

We also note that, although the evaluation targets the standard errors, 
the relative bias of the estimates was also computed, because standard errors 
of markedly biased estimates are of limited use for inference. It is reported 
in the text, but not in the figures.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-performance
#| tbl-cap: "Performance Measures for Evaluating the Standard Errors"
#| apa-note: "$\\hat\\theta_k$ is the estimate of parameter $\\theta$ in replication $k$ ($k = 1, \\dots, K$) and $\\bar{\\theta}$ the mean of the $K$ estimates. $\\widehat{SE}_k$ is the estimated standard error in replication $k$, $\\overline{SE} = \\tfrac{1}{K}\\sum_k \\widehat{SE}_k$, $\\overline{SE^2} = \\tfrac{1}{K}\\sum_k \\widehat{SE}_k^2$, and $L_k, U_k$ are the confidence interval limits. The subscript $(j)$ marks a leave-one-out jackknife replicate. The dash marks an MCSE that is not computed."
tab <- data.frame(
  measure = c("Relative bias", "SD", "SE/SD ratio", "SE$^2$/VAR ratio", "Coverage"),
  empirical = c("$(\\bar{\\theta}-\\theta)/\\theta$",
                "$S_{\\hat\\theta}=\\sqrt{\\tfrac{1}{K-1}\\sum_{k=1}^{K}(\\hat\\theta_k-\\bar{\\theta})^2}$",
                "$\\overline{SE}/S_{\\hat\\theta}$",
                "$\\nu=\\overline{SE^2}/S_{\\hat\\theta}^2$",
                "$c=\\tfrac{1}{K}\\sum_{k=1}^{K}I(L_k\\le\\theta\\le U_k)$"),
  mcse = c("$S_{\\hat\\theta}/(\\sqrt{K}\\,|\\theta|)$",
           "$\\sqrt{\\tfrac{K-1}{K}\\sum_{j=1}^{K}(S_{(j)}-S_{\\hat\\theta})^2}$",
           "---",
           "$\\sqrt{\\tfrac{K-1}{K}\\sum_{j=1}^{K}(\\nu_{(j)}-\\nu)^2}$",
           "$\\sqrt{c(1-c)/K}$"))
knitr::asis_output(paste0("\\begin{center}\n",
  knitr::kable(tab, booktabs = TRUE, escape = FALSE, longtable = TRUE,
               linesep = "", format = "latex",
               col.names = c("Performance measure", "Empirical calculation", "MCSE")),
  "\n\\end{center}"))
```

### Reproducibility and Computational Details

All analyses were conducted in R [@rcoreteam_2026] using the lavaan package
[@rosseel_2012] for estimation, simhelpers [@joshi_pustejovsky_2025] for
performance evaluation, and ggplot2 [@wickham_2016] for the figures. The
computational environment was pinned with Nix [@dolstra_etall_2004] via the
rix package [@rodrigues_baumann_2026], and a Dockerfile that builds the same
environment inside a container is also provided. The article was written
with the apaquarto extension [@schneider_2026]. For an extensive description 
of all files and how to reproduce the simulation study as well as the 
manuscript, see the repository.

```{r}
#| label: performance
source("performance_calculation.R")
pct <- function(x) sprintf("%.1f", 100 * x)
rb_other <- max(abs(summ$rel_bias[summ$estimator != "IV"]))
rb_iv100 <- summ[summ$estimator == "IV" & summ$n == 100 & summ$rel == 0.6, ]
rb_iv_load <- range(-rb_iv100$rel_bias[grepl("=~", rb_iv100$parameter)])
rb_iv_var <- range(rb_iv100$rel_bias[grepl("^eta[0-9]~~", rb_iv100$parameter)])
rb_300 <- max(abs(summ$rel_bias[summ$n >= 300]))
summ$estimator <- factor(summ$estimator, levels = c("JS", "JSA", "IV", "ML"))

## long format over the three criteria, with MCSE bars
crit <- c(sd = "SD", rb_var = "SE²/VAR", coverage = "Coverage")
long <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(crit), function(k)
  data.frame(summ[c("n", "rel", "estimator", "parameter")],
             criterion = crit[k], value = summ[[k]],
             mcse = summ[[paste0(k, "_mcse")]])))
long$criterion <- factor(long$criterion, levels = crit)
long$rel <- factor(long$rel, levels = rels,
                   labels = paste("Reliability", sub("^0", "", rels)))
long$lower <- long$value - long$mcse
long$upper <- long$value + long$mcse

## SE²/VAR values above `cap` are drawn at `cap` with an open triangle and no bar
cap <- 1.5
i <- long$criterion == "SE²/VAR"
long$clipped <- i & long$value > cap
long$value[long$clipped] <- cap
long$upper[i] <- pmin(long$upper[i], cap)
long$lower[long$clipped] <- long$upper[long$clipped] <- NA

ref <- data.frame(criterion = factor(c("SE²/VAR", "Coverage"), levels = crit),
                  y = c(1, 0.95))
pd <- position_dodge(width = 25)

plot_params <- function(pars, labels, breaks = ns) {
  v <- long[long$parameter %in% pars, ]
  v$parameter <- factor(v$parameter, levels = pars, labels = labels)
  ggplot(v, aes(n, value, colour = estimator, shape = estimator,
                linetype = estimator)) +
    geom_hline(data = ref, aes(yintercept = y), colour = "grey55",
               linetype = "dotted") +
    geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper), width = 0,
                  linetype = "solid", position = pd, na.rm = TRUE) +
    geom_line(linewidth = 0.5, position = pd) +
    geom_point(size = 2, position = pd) +
    geom_point(data = v[v$clipped, ], shape = 2, size = 3, position = pd,
               show.legend = FALSE) +
    facet_grid(rel + criterion ~ parameter, scales = "free_y", switch = "y",
               labeller = labeller(parameter = label_parsed)) +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = breaks) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c(JS = "#2a78d6", JSA = "#eda100",
                                   IV = "#eb6834", ML = "#1baf7a")) +
    scale_shape_manual(values = c(JS = 16, JSA = 18, IV = 15, ML = 17)) +
    scale_linetype_manual(values = c(JS = "solid", JSA = "dashed",
                                     IV = "longdash", ML = "dotdash")) +
    labs(x = expression(italic(n)), y = NULL, colour = "Estimator",
         shape = "Estimator", linetype = "Estimator") +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom", strip.placement = "outside",
          strip.text.y.left = element_text(angle = 90),
          panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
          panel.border = element_rect(fill = NA, colour = "grey80"))
}
pars_coef <- c("eta2~eta1", "eta3~eta1", "eta3~eta2")
lab_coef  <- c("B[21]", "B[31]", "B[32]")
pars_load <- c("eta1=~y2", "eta2=~y6", "eta3=~y10")
lab_load  <- c("lambda[2]", "lambda[6]", "lambda[10]")
pars_res  <- c("y1~~y1", "y2~~y2", "y5~~y5", "y6~~y6", "y9~~y9", "y10~~y10")
lab_res   <- c("theta[1]", "theta[2]", "theta[5]", "theta[6]", "theta[9]",
               "theta[10]")
pars_fvar <- c("eta1~~eta1", "eta2~~eta2", "eta3~~eta3")
lab_fvar  <- c("Var(eta[1])", "Var(zeta[2])", "Var(zeta[3])")
```

# Results

## Convergence, Outliers, and Inadmissible Solutions

All four estimators converged in every replication of every condition.
Outlier screening removed `r scr$removed` of the 18,000 replications
(`r sprintf("%.2f", scr$removed_pct)`%), concentrated at $n=100$ with
reliability .6, where `r sprintf("%.1f", scr$removed_by_cond[1])`% of the
replications were removed, flagged mainly through JS
(`r sprintf("%.1f", scr$flagged_100_06["JS"])`% of the replications in that
condition). In every other condition fewer than 0.5% of the replications were
removed. Inadmissible solutions occurred in `r scr$inad` replications, all
for JS at $n=100$ with reliability .6, where a disturbance variance
estimate was negative. All of them were also flagged by the outlier
screening, so none enters the results below.

## Relative Bias

JS, JSA, and ML were essentially unbiased, with absolute relative bias of at
most `r pct(rb_other)`% for any parameter and condition. MIIV was also nearly
unbiased except at reliability .6 and small samples. At $n=100$ its loadings
were slightly underestimated, by `r pct(rb_iv_load[1])` to
`r pct(rb_iv_load[2])`%, whereas its latent and disturbance variances were
overestimated by `r pct(rb_iv_var[1])` to `r pct(rb_iv_var[2])`%. From
$n=300$ onward, all estimators were within `r pct(rb_300)`% of the population
values.

## Standard Error Performance

Each figure presents reliability .6 in the upper half and .8 in the lower
half. @fig-sim-structural shows the latent regression slopes,
@fig-sim-loadings one loading per latent variable, @fig-sim-residual the
measurement error variances of the scaling indicators and one nonscaling 
indicator per latent variable, and @fig-sim-factorvar the variance of $\eta_1$ 
and the two disturbance variances. Omitted loadings and measurement error 
variances behave similarly to those shown for the same latent variable, with 
SE$^2$/VAR ratios that differ 
by at most 0.15 and coverage by .03 in every condition. Overall, standard
error performance was acceptable. Across all conditions,
estimators, and parameters, 
`r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * mean(summ$coverage >=.925 & summ$coverage <= .975))`% 
of coverage rates fell between .925 and .975
and `r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * mean(summ$rb_var >= .90 & summ$rb_var <= 1.10))`%
of SE$^2$/VAR ratios between 0.90 and 1.10, with no ratio below 0.90. From
$n=300$ onward, the few ratios above 1.10 remained below 1.12. Three
departures are concentrated at $n=100$ and $n=200$, mainly at reliability .6.

First, JS standard errors for $B_{31}$ and $B_{32}$ exceed the acceptable
range at reliability .6, with SE$^2$/VAR ratios of 1.5–1.6 at $n=100$ and
1.13–1.14 at $n=200$. Coverage nonetheless exceeds .975 only for $B_{31}$ at
$n=100$. Its SD is also the largest, 0.24 versus 0.13–0.17 at $n=100$. These
patterns may reflect instability in the reliability adjustment for the
$\eta_3$ equation. In some replications, the implied correlation between
$\eta_1$ and $\eta_2$ approaches 1, making the fitted predictors nearly
collinear and inflating both estimates and standard errors. Screening removed
the most extreme cases, but milder cases remain. JSA, which aggregates
indicators within each latent variable, shows no corresponding instability.

Second, MIIV loading intervals fall below the acceptable coverage range at
reliability .6, with coverage of .88–.90 at $n=100$, compared with .93–.96 for
the other estimators, despite SE$^2$/VAR ratios of 0.98–1.14 and the smallest
SD. This discrepancy reflects the downward loading bias reported above,
consistent with the weak instrument effect described by @jin_etall_2021, and
diminishes slowly as sample size increases.

Third, at $n=100$ MIIV overestimates the standard errors of the latent and
disturbance variances, with ratios of 1.11–1.18, but its coverage rates of
.96–.97 remain within the acceptable range. ML, in contrast, has ratios close
to 1 but coverage rates of .91–.94 for the disturbance variances. JS and JSA
fall between them. At reliability .8, the coverage rate for the disturbance
variance of $\eta_2$ is about .92 for ML, JS, and JSA, just below the
acceptable range. Measurement error variances show less contrast, with coverage rates
from .91 to .96 across estimators and a common dip at $n=100$.

```{r}
#| label: fig-sim-structural
```

# Discussion

This article presented JS and JSA estimation as implemented in the R
package lavaan, starting from a worked example and using MIIV as a point of
comparison within a common notation. It also developed and presented 
analytical standard errors for JS and JSA by applying the delta method to the 
complete estimation procedure. A reproducible simulation study then evaluated 
their accuracy against MIIV and ML under correct model specification.

The main finding is that the analytical standard errors of JS and JSA
performed comparably to those of MIIV and ML. Both estimators were
essentially unbiased in all conditions, and their coverage rates and
SE$^2$/VAR ratios were acceptable from $n=300$ onward for essentially
every parameter.
The one notable departure concerned JS at reliability .6 and $n\le200$,
where the standard errors of the slopes in the $\eta_3$ equation were too
large. This pattern appears to reflect instability in the reliability
adjustment when the fitted latent predictors are nearly collinear. JSA,
which aggregates indicators within each latent variable, showed no
corresponding instability. These results extend those of
@burghgraeve_etall_2021, who found JS less efficient than JSA for latent
regression estimation and JSA competitive with ML, consistent with the
empirical standard deviations observed here. Their bootstrap standard
errors for JS were too small in small samples, however, whereas our
analytical standard errors were too large. Whether this difference reflects
the standard error methods or differences in the simulation conditions
requires further investigation.

The MIIV results provide the contrast and broadly align with earlier
studies. @bollen_2018, summarizing @bollen_etall_2007, reports few
differences between MIIV and ML under correct specification with normally
distributed data. Our results agree in terms of bias and standard error
accuracy from $n=300$ onward, although MIIV remained less precise than ML
for the latent regression slopes. @jin_etall_2021 found that low scaling
indicator reliability can lead to biased MIIV estimates in small samples
and, under that condition, to the least accurate standard errors for the
variance parameters. Related patterns appeared here at reliability .6 and
$n=100$, with loading bias and undercoverage, alongside inflated standard
errors for latent and disturbance variances. JS and JSA showed neither the
loading bias nor the undercoverage in these conditions.

With this article and its simulation, we did not intend to compare the
approaches exhaustively. Given that JS and JSA have received little
attention so far, our aim was to show what they share with MIIV and that
both can perform comparably to ML. We hope this encourages further
evaluation of JS and JSA across a broader range of conditions, including
departures from normality and misspecification of the measurement and
latent variable models, where their equation-by-equation structure may
matter most.
